content: Black band disease is a condition that leads to the complete degradation of coral tissue. This degradation is caused by a pathogenic microbial consortium that manifests as a dark red or black microbial mat. This mat is typically located between healthy coral tissue and the freshly exposed coral skeleton. The color of the band can range from blackish-brown to red, depending on the vertical position of cyanobacterial populations within the band. This positioning is influenced by the light intensity-dependent photic response of cyanobacterial filaments. The color, which is due to the cyanobacterial pigment phycoerythrin, also depends on the thickness of the band. The band itself is approximately 1 mm thick and can vary in width from 1 mm to 7 cm. White specks may sometimes appear on the surface of the band, occasionally forming dense white patches. The microbial mat moves across coral colonies at rates ranging from 3 mm to 1 cm per day. Tissue death occurs as a result of exposure to an anoxic, sulfide-rich microenvironment at the base of the band. The microbial consortium responsible for black band disease consists of a synergistic community of photosynthetic and non-photosynthetic bacteria. This consortium includes three functionally and physically dominant members, along with numerous heterotrophic bacteria whose roles in the disease remain unclear. The three dominant members are populations of cyanobacteria, sulfide-oxidizing bacteria, and sulfate-reducing bacteria. Among these, the most well-known cyanobacterium is Phormidium corallyticum. Sulfide-oxidizing bacteria, primarily Beggiatoa species, are present in well-developed bands and exhibit visible vertical migrations within the band matrix. When present on the surface of the band, Beggiatoa appears white due to intracellular inclusions of stored elemental sulfur. Sulfate-reducing bacteria, dominated by Desulfovibrio species, are located at the base of the band and are responsible for producing high concentrations of sulfide within the band matrix. Microscopic examination of black band disease reveals motile (gliding) filaments of Phormidium corallyticum, which are 4 µm wide and have one rounded end and one sharply tapering end. Gliding Beggiatoa filaments, which are 1–4 µm wide, are also present. These filaments are non-pigmented but contain highly refractive intracellular granules of elemental sulfur. Additionally, numerous Gram-negative bacteria (small rods) are observed, though they cannot be identified using light microscopy. The functional role of this diverse bacterial population remains unknown. Black band disease affects 42 species of coral and has a worldwide distribution. The only known reservoir for the disease is within cyanobacterial biofilms found on sediments in depressions of healthy corals that are susceptible to black band disease.
